The problem

Where do decisions go to die?

When documentation lacks structure, three failure modes show up — every time.

Tribal knowledge

Critical context lives in heads. When people leave, it leaves with them.

Lost decisions

"Why did we choose X?" Nobody remembers. The Slack thread is gone. Git history doesn't say.

Slow onboarding

New engineers take weeks to ramp because the system is undocumented.

Structure beats archaeology.

Phases 1 → 3

Get started

An idea graduates into a project, gets justified, and ownership is established.

Phase 1 · Discovery

GitHub Issue

Small ideas live as issues. Only graduates to a doc if it becomes a project.

/issues/{N}
→
Phase 2 · Justify

Business Case

Scales: light usage = problem + reasons + risks. Heavy usage adds finance. Optional companion: Financial Model with NPV + sensitivity analysis.

Project-scoped document · resolve its exact path and filename from solution-structure
→
Phase 3 · Take Over

Takeover

When inheriting an existing system. Same template flips to Handover at Phase 9 closure.

Ticket-scoped document · resolve its exact path and filename from solution-structure
Phase 4

Decide & Design

Three artifacts that look similar but answer different questions. Pick the smallest set.

RFC

Should we do this?

Problem, alternatives, trade-offs. Open while under discussion; closes with a decision.

→
ADR

We chose X because Y.

Immutable record of one decision. Single-focus. Discoverable.

→
Design Doc

Here's how we'll build it.

Components, APIs, data flow, edge cases. Lives through implementation.

Default flow

Propose → Decide → Design how. Not strictly linear — pick the subset that fits the change.

ADRs are emergent

An ADR can crystallize during the RFC, during Design Doc work, or even after-the-fact during Implementation.

Phase 5 Phase 6

Build Contract → Implementation

Tests come before code. They are the contract, not the chaser.

Phase 5 · optional

Test Plan

Project / release-level test strategy. Environments, data, exit criteria. Required in regulated contexts (FDA, IEC 62304).

Skip for feature-by-feature work where TC + CI gates suffice.

Phase 5 · per-feature

Test Cases

Drafted before Developer starts, derived 1:1 from acceptance criteria. Catches missing or ambiguous criteria while still cheap to fix.

Phase 6

Implementation

Code is gated by Test Cases. No template — the tests are the contract.

tester drafts → developer builds → reviewer gates → tester tests
Phase 7 Phase 8 Phase 9

Operate, Report, Close

From "live in prod" to "wrap up and capture lessons."

Phase 7 · Operate

Runbook + SOP

Runbook: handle failures. On-call procedure. Symptom → Diagnosis → Mitigation → Rollback.

SOP: repeatable procedures. Compliance and consistency. Living, slug-only.

Phase 8 · Report

Project Status Update

Weekly / monthly stakeholder reporting. RAG status, RAID log, milestone tracker, budget update. Dated per report.

Phase 9 · Close

Handover + Retrospective

Handover: same template as Phase 3 Takeover, used outgoing here. Sign-off ceremony at the end.

Retrospective: Original Goals vs Actual Outcomes. What went well, what didn't, root causes, lessons, action items. Captures learnings for the next project.

Phase 10

The always-living layer

Four docs that are never closed — they evolve with the system. Each has a distinct update trigger.

Tech Stack Overview

Reference · DAMA-style index

Languages → Runtime → Frameworks → Storage → Caching → Messaging → Testing → Observability → CI/CD → Cloud.

Updated when an ADR changes a tech choice.

Architecture Overview

Diátaxis · Explanation

How the existing product / module / component / service / coherent area works. Multiple per repo — pick the narrowest scope that captures a useful audience.

Updated when behavior or structure shifts.

Data Dictionary

Reference · DAMA-DMBOK

Schema, types, constraints, lineage. PII classification. Source System per field — two sources, two rows.

Updated on any schema change. No ADR required.

Business Glossary

Reference · DAMA-DMBOK

Terms, acronyms, synonyms, business rules. Cross-team naming alignment.

Updated when terminology enters or shifts.

Orthogonal flows

Two flows that don't fit on the project timeline — they happen on their own clock.

Flow A · Incident · system-lifetime

Post Incident Review

Written after every incident. Severity, timeline, root cause, blast radius, what went well, what went wrong.

Where we got lucky

Google SRE convention. Documents near-misses to surface fragile systems before the next incident — luck doesn't compound.

Not project-bound. A project can close while PIRs continue.

Flow B · People · not in repo

Role Brief · Brag · PIP

HR-adjacent docs. Templates kept here for convenience; produced documents live outside the engineering repo.

Industry alignment

Frameworks behind the flow

This isn't invented — it aligns with three industry-standard bodies of knowledge.

Delivery Performance

DORA

DevOps Research and Assessment. Identifies the capabilities that drive software delivery performance and organizational outcomes.

Informs: the lifecycle's emphasis on Test Cases as build contract, Runbook for operate, PIR for incidents.
Data Governance

DAMA-DMBOK

Data Management Body of Knowledge (2nd ed.). Industry reference for data architecture, modeling, master data, metadata, and data quality.

Informs: Business Glossary structure (term, acronym, synonyms, owner) and Data Dictionary fields (PII, lineage, source).
Documentation Taxonomy

Diátaxis

Tutorial · How-to · Reference · Explanation. Each quadrant has its own audience and shape — conflating them produces docs that serve no one.

Informs: separating Architecture Overview (Explanation) from Runbook/SOP (How-to) from Glossary/Dictionary (Reference).

Conventions in 30 seconds

The rules that keep it consistent

If you remember these five, the rest follows.

1 · Physical naming authority
solution-structure

Resolve every in-repo scope, directory, filename, and attachment location from its canonical document catalog. Do not derive another naming pattern here.

2 · Doc ID inside the file
{DocumentTypeAbbreviation}-{yyyyMMddHHmm}-{slug}

e.g., `ADR-202604261430-adopt-event-sourcing-for-billing`. Lives in `## Metadata`, never in the H1.

3 · Date format
[YYYYMMDD]

Compact, no dashes. Times: `[HH:MM]` (24-hour).

4 · Metadata field order

Identity → Version (rare) → Last Updated → Date → Status → Domain fields → Person fields. By scanning priority, not alphabetical.

5 · DRY · the most-broken rule

Metadata is data, not links. Pointers to other docs go only in ## References — never as a **RFC:** / **Business Case:** field. One canonical location per fact.

solution-structure owns placement and names. Templates own document content; SKILL.md owns semantics and workflow.
